lessons.title: What is Linux, really?
lessons.body:
Linux is not a full operating system by itself - it is the KERNEL, the core program that talks to your hardware.

Think of a car: the kernel is the engine. You never drive an engine alone - you need seats, wheels, a steering wheel. A Linux distribution (distro) like Ubuntu or Fedora bundles the kernel with tools and apps so you can actually use it.

When people say 'I use Linux', they mean they use a distro built on the Linux kernel.
lessons.example:
$ uname -s
Linux

$ uname -r
6.8.0-example  <- kernel release varies by machine
lessons.scenario: When an app asks for memory, the kernel is the traffic controller that allocates it.

check.q: What talks to hardware for Linux apps?
check.e: The kernel manages CPU, memory and devices; the desktop is an app.

lessons.title: A 5-minute history
lessons.body:
1969: Ken Thompson and colleagues begin Unix at Bell Labs. Its licensing and history differ from the freely licensed Linux kernel.

1983: Richard Stallman starts the GNU project - free Unix-like tools for everyone.

1991: Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, writes a free kernel 'just for fun' and posts it online. GNU tools plus the Linux kernel power many distributions, though some (such as Android) use other user-space tools.

Now: Linux powers many supercomputers, servers, cloud machines and Android devices. Exact market shares change.
lessons.example:
$ uname -s
Linux

$ cat /etc/os-release | head -2
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
(sample output; your distro can differ)
lessons.scenario: A Linux web server and an Android phone both use a Linux kernel, but their apps and tools differ.

check.q: What did Torvalds publish in 1991?
check.e: The kernel came first; a distro adds user-space tools.

lessons.title: Distros: one kernel, many flavors
lessons.body:
A distribution = Linux kernel + package manager + default apps + a philosophy.

Debian family (Ubuntu, Mint): apt, .deb packages, beginner friendly.
Red Hat family (RHEL, Fedora, AlmaLinux): dnf/yum, .rpm packages, common in companies.
Arch: rolling release, always newest, for enthusiasts.

Interview tip: companies run servers on RHEL-like or Ubuntu LTS systems, so learn apt AND dnf basics.
lessons.diagram:
Linux kernel
                  |
   +----------+---+---------+
   |          |           |
 Debian     Red Hat      Arch
   |          |           |
 Ubuntu    Fedora      Manjaro
 Mint      AlmaLinux
lessons.example:
$ cat /etc/os-release | grep -E "^(ID|ID_LIKE)="
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
(sample; ID_LIKE may be absent)
lessons.scenario: A .deb package points you toward the Debian family, while a .rpm often points toward Fedora or RHEL.

check.q: Which family commonly uses apt?
check.e: Remember apt with Debian and Ubuntu; dnf with Fedora and RHEL.

lessons.title: Why companies love Linux
lessons.body:
Linux is open source: its source code is available under licenses that allow use, modification and distribution under their terms. Many distributions are available without a license fee; paid support also exists.

Strong permissions, regular updates and careful administration matter more than assuming that open source is automatically secure.

Commands and scripts make routine system administration easier to repeat.
lessons.example:
$ uname -r
5.15.0-91-generic        <- your kernel version

$ cat /etc/os-release
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION="22.04 LTS"    <- your distro
lessons.scenario: An admin can save a repeated check as a script and run it the same way each time.

check.q: Does publicly readable source code guarantee a secure server?
o: No, it still needs updates and good setup
check.e: Open code can be reviewed, but security still needs patching and careful setup.

lessons.title: One tree, one root
lessons.body:
Windows has many drives (C:, D:). Linux presents ONE directory tree starting at / (called 'root').

Mounted disks and many device interfaces appear within this tree. Filesystem volumes are 'mounted' (attached) into folders of the tree instead of getting letters.

Once this clicks, everything else in Linux gets easier.
lessons.diagram:
/  <- root, the top of everything
|-- home/     <- users live here (/home/akash)
|-- etc/      <- configuration files
|-- var/      <- logs and changing data
|-- usr/      <- installed programs
|-- tmp/      <- temporary files (cleanup varies)
|-- dev/      <- hardware as files (/dev/sda = disk)
|-- proc/     <- live kernel info (virtual)
|-- root/     <- home of the admin user
lessons.example:
$ pwd
/home/akash
$ ls /
bin  dev  etc  home  proc  tmp  usr  var
(sample output; folders vary)
lessons.scenario: An external drive mounted at /mnt/usb appears inside the same tree as your home folder.

check.q: Where does the Linux directory tree start?
check.e: / is the root of the one visible directory tree.

lessons.title: pwd, cd, ls - your three best friends
lessons.body:
pwd = 'where am I?' (print working directory).

cd = 'go somewhere' (change directory). cd /etc goes to /etc, cd .. goes UP one level, cd ~ (or just cd) goes home, cd - goes BACK to where you were.

ls = 'show me what is here'. ls -l shows details, ls -a shows hidden dotfiles, ls -lh shows sizes in K/M/G.
lessons.example:
$ pwd
/home/akash

$ cd /etc/nginx
$ pwd
/etc/nginx

$ cd ..          <- up one level
$ cd ~           <- back home

$ ls -lh
-rw-r--r-- 1 akash akash 4.0K notes.txt
lessons.scenario: If your prompt says /home/akash, `cd ..` takes you to /home.

check.q: Which command tells you your current directory?
check.e: pwd prints the working directory; ls lists entries.

lessons.title: Absolute vs relative paths
lessons.body:
An ABSOLUTE path starts from root: /home/akash/docs/report.txt. It works from anywhere.

A RELATIVE path starts from where you stand: if you are in /home/akash, then docs/report.txt means /home/akash/docs/report.txt.

Special shortcuts: . = this directory, .. = parent directory, ~ = my home.

Rule of thumb: in scripts, avoid assuming a working directory; use absolute paths or derive paths from the script location.
lessons.diagram:
you are here: /home/akash

absolute:  /var/log/syslog   (full address)
relative:  ../../var/log/syslog (directions
           from where you stand)

.  = /home/akash   (here)
.. = /home         (one up)
lessons.example:
$ cd /tmp
$ pwd
/tmp
$ readlink -f ./demo/../note.txt
/tmp/note.txt
(sample: path normalization by GNU readlink -f)
lessons.scenario: From /home/akash, docs/note.txt means /home/akash/docs/note.txt.

check.q: Which path is absolute?
check.e: The initial / anchors a path at the root.

lessons.title: Hidden files and finding things
lessons.body:
Files starting with a dot are hidden: .bashrc, .ssh/. They are normal files - ls just hides them by default. Config for your user usually lives in dotfiles at home.

find = slow but precise search of real files right now.
locate/plocate = fast search of a periodically refreshed index (updatedb refreshes it). It may not be installed and the index can be stale.
lessons.example:
$ ls -a ~
.bashrc  .profile  .ssh  notes.txt

$ find /etc -name '*.conf'
/etc/resolv.conf
/etc/sysctl.conf

$ locate nginx.conf
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf
lessons.scenario: To find your hidden shell config, use `ls -a ~`; normal ls hides .bashrc.

check.q: Why might plain ls omit .bashrc?
o: Its name starts with a dot
check.e: Dot-prefixed names are hidden from default directory listings.

lessons.title: Create, copy, move, delete
lessons.body:
mkdir makes directories (mkdir -p a/b/c makes the whole chain).

touch makes an empty file (or refreshes its timestamp).

cp copies: cp file backup.txt, cp -r dir1 dir2 for folders.

mv moves AND renames - same command, two jobs.

rm normally bypasses the desktop Trash. There is no built-in undo; backups may still exist. Always read the command twice before pressing Enter, especially with rm -r or rm -rf.
lessons.example:
$ mkdir -p projects/demo
$ touch projects/demo/readme.txt
$ cp projects/demo/readme.txt backup.txt
$ mv backup.txt projects/
$ rm -r projects/demo   <- removed without Trash; restore from backup if needed
lessons.scenario: Copy a report before editing it: `cp report.txt report.bak` keeps the original.

check.q: Which command copies a file without removing its source?
check.e: cp copies; mv moves or renames.

lessons.title: Links: shortcuts, Linux style
lessons.body:
A SOFT link (symlink) is like a Windows shortcut - a signpost to another path. Delete the original and the signpost points nowhere (broken link).

A HARD link is a second NAME for the exact same data (same inode). Delete the original name and the data still lives under the other name.

ln -s target linkname makes a symlink; ln target linkname makes a hard link.
lessons.diagram:
symlink:   link.s --> /real/file.txt --> DATA
           (delete file.txt: link.s breaks)

hard link: name1 --+
                   +--> inode 4392 --> DATA
           name2 --+
           (delete name1: data survives)
lessons.example:
$ mkdir -p /tmp/linux-practice && cd /tmp/linux-practice
$ printf "hello\n" > original.txt
$ ln original.txt alias.txt
$ ln -s original.txt shortcut.txt
$ ls -li original.txt alias.txt
4392 -rw-r--r-- ... alias.txt
4392 -rw-r--r-- ... original.txt
(sample inode and metadata; try in a disposable directory)
lessons.scenario: Point a shortcut at a changing config path with a symlink; a hard link is another name for the same inode.

check.q: Which link can point across filesystems?
check.e: A symlink stores a path; a hard link shares the original inode.

lessons.title: Find anything: find and du
lessons.body:
find walks the real directory tree: find / -name 'error.log' searches by name, find /home -size +100M hunts big files.

du -sh folder tells you how much space a folder eats - the first command to run when a disk fills up.

file tells you what a file REALLY is, ignoring its extension.
lessons.example:
$ find /var/log -name '*.log' -size +50M
/var/log/bigapp/debug.log

$ du -sh /var/log/*
4.0K   /var/log/apt
812M   /var/log/bigapp

$ file mystery
mystery: PDF document, version 1.4
lessons.scenario: When logs fill a drive, `du -sh /var/log` shows the folder size.

check.q: Which command summarizes directory disk usage?
check.e: du measures files in a folder; df reports filesystem free space.

lessons.title: rm -rf: the command to respect
lessons.body:
rm -r descends recursively; -f suppresses many prompts and ignores missing files. Be very careful with paths. GNU rm protects the literal filesystem root by default, but a typo elsewhere can delete important data.

Safety habits: inspect the target with ls, use tab completion, quote path variables and never assume they are set. In a script: : "${DIR:?set a nonempty directory}" before operating on "$DIR". Test destructive scripts against disposable files first.
lessons.diagram:
rm -rf /tmp/old     <- deletes that directory
rm -rf / tmp/old    <- wrong: root is a separate argument
          ^
GNU rm normally refuses the literal /, but do not count on it for other wrong paths.
lessons.example:
$ mkdir -p /tmp/linux-practice
$ touch /tmp/linux-practice/old.txt
$ ls /tmp/linux-practice
old.txt
$ rm -i /tmp/linux-practice/old.txt
rm: remove regular empty file "/tmp/linux-practice/old.txt"? n
(answer n to keep it; practice only with disposable files)
lessons.scenario: A typo in a delete command can remove the wrong folder. Recheck with ls before any rm.

check.q: Does rm -rf move files to a Trash folder?
check.e: rm bypasses the desktop Trash; restore from a backup if needed.

lessons.title: Reading files: cat, less, head, tail
lessons.body:
cat dumps the whole file - fine for short files.

less opens a pager: scroll with arrows, search with /word, quit with q. This is how pros read logs.

head shows the first lines, tail the last. tail -f is magic: it FOLLOWS a file and shows new lines live - perfect for watching logs while debugging.
lessons.example:
$ head -n 5 /var/log/syslog
Sep 27 08:01 server sshd[911]: ...

$ tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
192.168.1.5 - - [27/Sep] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200
<- new lines appear here in real time
lessons.scenario: When a service fails, `tail -n 20 app.log` shows the latest log lines.

check.q: Which command follows new log lines?
check.e: -f means follow as lines arrive.

lessons.title: Pipes and redirection
lessons.body:
Small tools, combined. That is the Unix philosophy.

| (pipe) sends one command's output into the next command's input.

> writes output to a file (overwrites). >> appends. 2> captures errors.

With just these, you can build powerful one-liners from simple tools.
lessons.diagram:
ps aux | grep nginx | awk '{print $2}'

ps aux        ->  all processes
grep nginx    ->  only nginx lines
awk '{print $2}' -> only the PID column

command  > out.txt   (overwrite)
command >> out.txt   (append)
command 2> err.txt   (errors only)
lessons.example:
$ printf "one\ntwo\n" | grep two
two

$ printf "old\n" > demo.txt
$ printf "new\n" >> demo.txt
$ cat demo.txt
old
new
(disposable demo.txt in your practice folder)
lessons.scenario: To save new output without replacing old output, `>>` adds to a log.

check.q: Which redirects stdout by appending?
check.e: Two greater-than signs append; one overwrites.

lessons.title: grep: find needles in haystacks
lessons.body:
grep PATTERN FILE prints lines matching the pattern.

Daily flags: -i ignore case, -r search folders recursively, -n show line numbers, -v show NON-matching lines, -c count matches.

90% of log debugging is: tail -f the log, or grep -i 'error' the log.
lessons.example:
$ grep -in 'failed' /var/log/auth.log
812:Sep 27 09:12 sshd: Failed password for root

$ grep -ri 'timeout' /etc/nginx/
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf: keepalive_timeout 65;
lessons.scenario: Filter a large log with `grep -i failed app.log` regardless of case.

check.q: Which grep flag ignores case?
check.e: -i means case-insensitive; -v means invert match.

lessons.title: cut, sort, uniq, wc: data crunching
lessons.body:
cut extracts columns (cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd lists all usernames).

sort orders lines (sort -n for numbers, sort -h for human sizes).

uniq collapses duplicate lines - sort first when counting duplicates across the whole file; uniq merges only ADJACENT duplicates.

wc -l counts lines: 'how many users?' = wc -l /etc/passwd.
lessons.example:
$ cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | head -3
backup
bash
bin

$ history | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
    120 ls
     80 cd
     61 grep   <- your most used commands
lessons.scenario: Count repeated error types with `sort errors.txt | uniq -c`.

check.q: Why sort before uniq -c?
check.e: Sort groups matching lines together; uniq only sees neighbors.

lessons.title: Users and groups in plain words
lessons.body:
Every person (and many services) gets a USER. Users are collected into GROUPS so you can give a whole team access at once.

/etc/passwd = the list of users (name, UID, home, shell).
/etc/shadow = password hashes - restricted to privileged readers, not proof that hashes cannot be stolen.
/etc/group = the list of groups.

root (UID 0) is the superuser: it can do anything - which is why we use sudo instead of living as root.
lessons.example:
$ whoami
akash

$ id
uid=1000(akash) gid=1000(akash) groups=1000(akash),27(sudo)

$ getent passwd akash
akash:x:1000:1000:Akash,,,:/home/akash:/bin/bash
lessons.scenario: A web server account can belong to a shared group without sharing a password.

check.q: Which local file usually lists usernames and UIDs?
check.e: passwd holds user records; shadow holds restricted password hashes.

lessons.title: Reading rwx like a book
lessons.body:
Every file has three sets of permissions: OWNER, GROUP, OTHERS. Each set has three letters: r (read), w (write), x (execute/enter).

-rw-r--r-- reads: regular file; owner can read+write; group and others can only read.

drwxr-xr-x reads: directory; owner can do everything; group and others can enter and list names, but cannot change the directory itself under ordinary mode bits.

On a directory, x means 'may enter' - without it you cannot cd in, even with r.
lessons.diagram:
- rw- r-- r--
|  |   |   |
|  |   |   +-- others: read only
|  |   +------ group:  read only
|  +---------- owner:  read + write
+------------- regular file (d=dir, l=link)

r=4  w=2  x=1  ->  7=rwx  6=rw-  5=r-x  4=r--
lessons.example:
$ ls -ld /tmp
drwxrwxrwt ... /tmp

$ stat -c "%a %n" /tmp
1777 /tmp
(example; trailing t is the sticky bit)
lessons.scenario: A team can read a file with mode 640 if they are in its owning group; others cannot.

check.q: In rwx, what does x mean on a directory?
check.e: Directory x permits traversal, which cd needs.

lessons.title: chmod and chown
lessons.body:
chmod changes PERMISSIONS: chmod 755 script.sh (owner rwx, others rx) or chmod +x script.sh (just add execute).

chown changes OWNERSHIP: chown akash:developers file.txt.

Numbers are just sums: r=4, w=2, x=1. 6 = 4+2 = rw. 5 = 4+1 = r-x.

Classic setups: 644 for normal files, 755 for scripts and directories, 600 for private keys.
lessons.example:
$ chmod +x deploy.sh
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   <- ssh refuses loose keys
$ sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/index.html
lessons.scenario: A script with chmod 755 can be executed by owner, group and others.

check.q: What does chmod change?
check.e: chmod changes mode; chown changes ownership.

lessons.title: sudo: borrowed superpowers
lessons.body:
sudo runs ONE command as root: sudo apt update. Every use is logged - companies love that.

Who may sudo is decided in /etc/sudoers, edited ONLY with visudo (it syntax-checks before saving; a typo in sudoers can lock everyone out).

On Ubuntu, members of the 'sudo' group may sudo: usermod -aG sudo akash adds him (the -a matters: without it you REPLACE his groups).
lessons.diagram:
normal user --- sudo command ---> runs as root
                    |
              logged in /var/log/auth.log

/etc/sudoers:  akash  ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
               ^user  ^can run anything
lessons.example:
$ sudo -l
Matching Defaults entries for akash ...
User akash may run the following commands ...
(sample output, and only if sudo is configured)
lessons.scenario: An admin uses sudo apt update for one privileged command instead of staying root all day.

check.q: What does sudo do by default when allowed?
check.e: sudo runs a command as root by default, subject to its policy.

lessons.title: What is a process?
lessons.body:
A process is a running program. One application can run one or many processes.

Each process has a PID (process ID) and a parent (PPID). On a systemd-based host, PID 1 is systemd. A designated subreaper may adopt some orphaned processes.

See them: ps aux for a snapshot, top (or htop) for a live view. q quits top.
lessons.diagram:
systemd (PID 1)
  |-- sshd (PID 800)
  |     |-- bash (PID 901)   <- your shell
  |           |-- top (PID 950)
  |-- nginx (PID 820)
  |-- cron (PID 700)
lessons.example:
$ ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p $$
    PID    PPID COMMAND
   1234    123 bash
(sample PIDs vary; $$ is this shell)
lessons.scenario: If a web server has three workers, ps can show three process IDs.

check.q: What is PID?
check.e: Every running process has a PID; PPID points to its parent.

lessons.title: Signals: talking to processes
lessons.body:
A signal is a short message to a process.

SIGTERM (15) = 'please shut down cleanly' - what plain kill sends.
SIGKILL (9) = 'die NOW' - cannot be ignored, unsaved work is lost. Last resort.
SIGINT (2) = Ctrl+C.
SIGTSTP = Ctrl+Z (pause).

kill PID sends TERM; kill -9 PID forces. pkill nginx kills by name.
lessons.example:
$ ps aux | grep python
akash  4242  3.0  ... python app.py

$ kill 4242        <- polite stop
$ kill -9 4242     <- force, only if stuck
$ kill -l | head   <- list all signals
lessons.scenario: Ask a stuck service to stop cleanly with kill PID before trying kill -9.

check.q: What signal does plain kill send?
check.e: TERM asks for a clean exit; KILL cannot be caught.

lessons.title: Background jobs: &, jobs, fg, bg
lessons.body:
Append & to start something in the background: ./backup.sh & - your prompt stays free.

jobs lists this shell's background work ([1] Running ...).

fg %1 pulls job 1 back to the foreground. bg %1 resumes a paused job in the background.

Ctrl+Z pauses the foreground program - handy when you started something big and forgot &.

Jobs may get SIGHUP when the shell exits; nohup ignores that signal and tmux/screen can keep a session. Use a service manager for reliable background services.
lessons.example:
$ ./long-scan.sh &
[1] 5001
$ jobs
[1]+  Running  ./long-scan.sh &
$ fg %1     <- bring it back
lessons.scenario: Put a slow read-only scan in the background with `find /tmp -name "*.log" &`.

check.q: How do you bring job 1 to the foreground?
check.e: fg = foreground; bg = background.

lessons.title: Priorities and system health
lessons.body:
nice sets how polite a process is about CPU: -20 (greedy, root only) to 19 (very polite). Start nice: nice -n 10 ./heavy.sh. Change later: renice 5 -p 4242.

Health check trio:
uptime - 1/5/15-minute load averages (runnable and uninterruptible tasks; compare with CPU count, but high load may also mean I/O waits).
free -h - memory and swap.
df -h - disk space.

These three are a quick starting point, not a full health check.
lessons.example:
$ uptime
 09:30:01 up 12 days, load average: 0.42, 0.35, 0.30

$ free -h
Mem:   total 7.7Gi   used 3.1Gi   available 4.2Gi
Swap:  total 2.0Gi   used  12Mi
lessons.scenario: When an app is slow, compare uptime load with CPU count and look for I/O waits.

check.q: Which command shows RAM and swap in readable units?
check.e: free shows memory; df shows filesystem space.

lessons.title: Why package managers are magic
lessons.body:
Installing software by hand means: download, unpack, resolve its dependencies (other packages it needs), copy files, update, remove cleanly... painful.

A package manager does ALL of that in one command, from trusted repositories (repos) - servers full of tested packages.

Debian/Ubuntu: apt with .deb files. RHEL/Fedora: dnf (yum is an older related command) with .rpm files. Arch: pacman.
lessons.diagram:
you:  sudo apt install nginx
                    |
                    v
   repo server (packages + metadata)
                    |
      downloads nginx + its dependencies
                    |
        installs files in the right places
                    |
         tracks everything for clean removal
lessons.example:
$ command -v apt
/usr/bin/apt
$ apt show bash | head -3
Package: bash
Version: 5.2...
(sample Debian/Ubuntu output; this only reads metadata)
lessons.scenario: For a web server, apt install nginx gets nginx plus its required libraries.

check.q: Which family uses .deb packages with apt?
check.e: apt works with Debian-family packages.

lessons.title: apt: your daily four
lessons.body:
sudo apt update - refresh the catalog (what versions exist). It does not upgrade installed packages; it may update local package lists and trigger related hooks.

sudo apt upgrade - install the newer versions. run update before upgrade to use the latest catalog.

sudo apt install nginx - install something new, dependencies included.

sudo apt remove nginx - uninstall (configs stay). apt purge also deletes configs. apt autoremove cleans orphaned dependencies.
lessons.example:
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
...
$ apt show nginx | head -4
Package: nginx
Version: 1.18.0-0ubuntu1
$ dpkg -l | grep nginx   <- is it installed?
lessons.scenario: Run apt update to refresh the menu, then apt upgrade to install newer versions.

check.q: Does apt update itself upgrade installed packages?
check.e: Update refreshes the catalog; upgrade installs updates.

lessons.title: dnf / rpm on the Red Hat side
lessons.body:
Interviews love asking both families - here is the mirror:

apt install  ->  dnf install
apt remove   ->  dnf remove
apt update   ->  dnf makecache (refresh metadata)
dpkg -l      ->  rpm -qa (query all)
dpkg -i x.deb ->  rpm -ivh x.rpm (neither resolves all dependencies)

Which package owns /usr/bin/curl? dpkg -S (Debian) or rpm -qf (Red Hat).
lessons.example:
$ sudo dnf install httpd -y
$ rpm -qa | grep httpd
httpd-2.4.57-1.el9.x86_64
$ rpm -qf /usr/sbin/httpd
httpd-2.4.57-1.el9.x86_64
lessons.scenario: On Fedora, use dnf install httpd rather than apt install httpd.

check.q: Which package file format is typical on RHEL?
check.e: RHEL/Fedora use RPM files and dnf.

lessons.title: When packages fight: fixing breakage
lessons.body:
Half-finished installs leave 'broken dependencies'. One possible fix is sudo apt --fix-broken install (apt -f install) - apt computes what to add or remove to heal the system.

APT sources can live in /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ (.list or .sources) - check there when a package is 'not found'.

Snaps and Flatpaks offer cross-distro packaging with configurable sandboxing - useful for desktop apps, less so for servers.
lessons.example:
$ sudo apt --fix-broken install
Reading package lists... Done
The following packages will be REMOVED: ...
$ cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list
lessons.scenario: If apt complains about unmet dependencies, inspect the proposed apt --fix-broken install changes before agreeing.

check.q: What does apt --fix-broken install try to repair?
check.e: It proposes package changes to restore consistent dependencies.

lessons.title: ip: your network x-ray
lessons.body:
ip addr (short: ip a) shows your interfaces and their IP addresses.

ip route shows where traffic goes - the 'default via ...' line is your gateway (the router).

The old command was ifconfig - know it, but use ip.

Quick check when the network 'is down': ip a (do I have an IP?) -> ip route (do I have a gateway?) -> ping the gateway -> ping 8.8.8.8 -> ping google.com.
lessons.example:
$ ip a
2: eth0: inet 192.168.1.50/24 ...

$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
lessons.scenario: If a server has an IP but no default route, it may reach its LAN but not other networks.

check.q: Which command shows the routing table?
check.e: route means where packets go; addr shows interface addresses.

lessons.title: ping, DNS and the /etc/hosts trick
lessons.body:
ping 8.8.8.8 tests raw connectivity (numbers). ping google.com ALSO tests DNS (names). If a numeric target responds but a hostname does not resolve, check DNS: look at /etc/resolv.conf.

DNS = the internet's phone book: name -> IP, on port 53. dig google.com shows the full answer.

/etc/hosts provides local mappings; lookup order is configurable in /etc/nsswitch.conf. Admins add test entries there; malware also abuses it.
lessons.diagram:
browser:  google.com ?
             |
   /etc/hosts? --yes--> use that IP
      | no
   DNS server (53) --> 142.250.x.x
             |
        connection!
lessons.example:
$ getent hosts localhost
::1  localhost
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf | head -3
nameserver 127.0.0.53
(sample; order and resolver vary)
lessons.scenario: If ping 8.8.8.8 works but a hostname does not resolve, inspect resolver settings.

check.q: Which local file can map a hostname to an IP?
check.e: hosts maps names; fstab lists mounts.

lessons.title: Ports and services: who is listening?
lessons.body:
A port is a numbered door on an IP address. IP = building, port = apartment.

Famous doors: 22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 53 DNS, 3306 MySQL.

ss -tuln lists listening TCP and bound UDP sockets (t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening/bound, n=numeric). If the web site is down but nginx runs, ss tells you whether anything listens on 80 at all.

A firewall (ufw, firewalld) decides which doors are open to the world.
lessons.example:
$ ss -tuln
Netid State  Local Address:Port
tcp   LISTEN 0.0.0.0:22
tcp   LISTEN 0.0.0.0:80

$ sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
$ sudo ufw enable
lessons.scenario: A web server listens on port 80 for HTTP and often 443 for HTTPS.

check.q: Which command lists listening TCP sockets numerically?
check.e: ss shows sockets; -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric.

lessons.title: ssh: your remote hands
lessons.body:
ssh user@server logs you into a remote machine, encrypted. This is THE daily tool of every admin.

scp file user@server:/path copies files over the same encrypted channel.

Port changed? ssh -p 2222 user@server (lowercase p for ssh, CAPITAL P for scp - classic interview trap).
lessons.example:
$ ssh akash@192.168.1.10
akash@server:~$ hostname
server

$ scp report.pdf akash@192.168.1.10:/tmp/
report.pdf   100%  220KB
lessons.scenario: Use ssh akash@server to log in securely; use scp for an encrypted file copy.

check.q: What is the usual SSH server port?
check.e: 22 is the conventional SSH port; servers can change it.

lessons.title: df and du: the space detectives
lessons.body:
'Disk full' is the most common server emergency ever. Two commands solve it:

df -h shows each FILESYSTEM's total/used/free - tells you WHICH disk is full.

du -sh /some/dir shows one folder's size - tells you WHAT ate it. Combine with sort to find the biggest folders.

Also watch inodes (df -i): millions of tiny files can fill a disk's file-index while space remains.
lessons.example:
$ df -h
/dev/sda1  50G  49G  0G  100% /

$ du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail -3
1.2G  /var/lib
6.8G  /var/log   <- found the eater
lessons.scenario: If df shows a full disk, du can help find which folder uses the space.

check.q: Which command shows filesystem free space?
check.e: df is disk free per filesystem; du measures file usage.

lessons.title: mount: attaching disks to the tree
lessons.body:
A new disk is invisible until you: partition it (fdisk/parted), format it (mkfs.ext4), and MOUNT it (attach it to a folder): mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data.

umount detaches (yes, one 'n'). It refuses while files are open - find the holders with lsof or fuser.

/etc/fstab lists mounts to apply at boot. Use UUIDs there (from blkid) because /dev/sdb can become /dev/sdc after a reboot.
lessons.example:
$ lsblk
sdb    8:16  0  100G  0 disk
+-sdb1 8:17  0 100G  0 part

$ sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
$ sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
$ blkid /dev/sdb1
/dev/sdb1: UUID="9f3a-..."  <- put this in fstab
lessons.scenario: Mounting a USB filesystem at /mnt/usb makes its files accessible at that path.

check.q: Which file lists configured mounts at boot?
check.e: fstab is the filesystem table; verify entries before reboot.

lessons.title: LVM: flexible storage
lessons.body:
Plain partitions are rigid: want it bigger later? Painful.

LVM adds a flexible layer: Physical Volumes (disks) pool into a Volume Group, and you carve Logical Volumes from the pool - often grow them online if the filesystem supports it and space is available. Shrinking may require unmounting or may be unsupported.

Grow in two steps: lvextend -L +10G /dev/data/web (bigger LV), then resize2fs /dev/data/web (grow the ext4 inside).
lessons.diagram:
/dev/sdb  /dev/sdc
   |          |
 pvcreate   pvcreate
   +----+----+
        v
   VG 'data'  (vgcreate)
        |
  +-----+------+
  |            |
 LV 'web'    LV 'db'   (lvcreate)
  |            |
 mkfs.ext4  mkfs.ext4
lessons.example:
$ lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,MOUNTPOINTS
NAME  SIZE TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda   100G disk
sda1  100G part /
(sample only: inspect before any disk changes; do not run pvcreate on a real disk for practice)
lessons.scenario: LVM can pool two spare disks into one volume group, then carve separate web and db volumes.

check.q: Which ordering describes LVM layers?
check.e: Physical Volumes pool into a Volume Group, then Logical Volumes are carved out.

lessons.title: RAID and inodes
lessons.body:
RAID 1 = mirroring: two disks hold identical data, one disk can fail while a healthy mirror retains data, but corruption or another failure can still lose data. RAID 0 = striping: speed, but one disk dying kills everything. RAID is NOT backup - rm deletes from both disks instantly!

An inode is a file's ID card: permissions, owner, timestamps, where the data blocks are. The NAME is stored separately in the directory, pointing at the inode - that is why hard links (two names, one inode) work.
lessons.diagram:
RAID 1 (mirror):        RAID 0 (stripe):
disk1 == disk2          disk1 + disk2 = fast
one dies, you survive   one dies, all lost

inode 4392: { perms, owner, size, blocks }
  ^        ^
  |        |
name1    name2   (hard links)
lessons.example:
$ df -i /
Filesystem  Inodes  IUsed  IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/sda1  100000  6000  94000   6% /
(sample; this checks inode usage without changing disks)
lessons.scenario: RAID 1 keeps a second disk copy, but accidentally deleting a file affects both copies.

check.q: Is a RAID 1 mirror a replacement for backups?
check.e: A mirror tolerates a disk failure, not deletion or corruption.

lessons.title: Your first script in 2 minutes
lessons.body:
A script is commands in a file, run top to bottom.

1. For a script to run directly under bash: start with #!/bin/bash (the shebang). Alternatively, run bash myscript.sh without an executable bit.
2. Make it runnable: chmod +x myscript.sh.
3. Run it: ./myscript.sh.

Comments start with #. Write them - future-you says thanks.
lessons.example:
#!/bin/bash
# Say hello and show the date

echo "Hello, Akash!"
date

$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh
Hello, Akash!
Sun Sep 27 13:50:00 IST 2026
lessons.scenario: Save two repeatable read-only checks in hello.sh and run it instead of retyping them.

check.q: What does #!/bin/bash at the start select?
check.e: The shebang tells the OS what runs the script directly.

lessons.title: Variables and arguments
lessons.body:
Variables: NAME=value (NO spaces around =), read with $NAME. Quote on use: "$NAME" keeps spaces safe.

Command substitution: TODAY=$(date +%F) captures a command's output.

Arguments: $1, $2 are what you pass after the script name; $# is how many; $@ is all of them; $0 is the script's own name.

$? holds the last command's exit code: 0 = success, anything else = failure.
lessons.example:
#!/bin/bash
NAME=$1
echo "Backup for $NAME"
mkdir -p "backups/$NAME"
echo "args: $# | last exit code: $?"

$ ./backup.sh website
Backup for website
args: 1 | last exit code: 0
lessons.scenario: If your file is named "my report", `"$1"` preserves it as one argument.

check.q: What does $# mean in a bash script?
check.e: # counts arguments; $? is the last command status.

lessons.title: Decisions: if, test, case
lessons.body:
if [ condition ]; then ... fi makes choices.

String test: [ "$a" = "yes" ]. Number tests: -eq -ne -lt -gt. File tests: -f (file exists), -d (directory), -x (executable). Mind the spaces inside [ ] - they are required.

For menus (start|stop|restart) case is cleaner than many ifs.
lessons.scenario: A backup script can check `[ -f file ]` before trying to read it.

check.q: Which test checks an ordinary file?
check.e: -f tests regular files; -d tests directories.

lessons.title: Loops and real-world script hygiene
lessons.body:
for name in list; do ...; done repeats per item. while condition; do ...; done repeats while true - while read -r line is THE way to process a file line by line.

Pro habits:
set -e at the top: exit on many unhandled errors, with important exceptions in conditions and &&/|| chains; test failures explicitly.
bash -x script.sh: trace mode - prints every command as it runs; your best debugging friend.
Quote every variable: "$file" not $file - spaces in names break unquoted scripts.
lessons.example:
while read -r user; do
  echo "Checking $user"
done < users.txt

for srv in web1 web2 db1; do
  ping -c1 "$srv" > /dev/null && echo "$srv OK"
done
lessons.scenario: Use `while IFS= read -r line` so spaces and backslashes in a file line survive.

check.q: Which option prints bash commands as they execute?
check.e: -x traces commands; -e changes many error-exit cases.

lessons.title: How a Linux machine boots
lessons.body:
Power on -> firmware (BIOS/UEFI) checks hardware and finds a bootable disk -> the bootloader (GRUB) loads the kernel into memory -> the kernel starts PID 1: systemd -> systemd starts all services in parallel (network, ssh, nginx...) -> login prompt.

Knowing this chain tells you WHERE to debug: no GRUB = disk/bootloader issue; GRUB but no login = service issue.
lessons.diagram:
POWER
  |
  v
BIOS/UEFI (firmware)
  |
  v
GRUB (bootloader)
  |
  v
Linux kernel
  |
  v
systemd (PID 1) ----> sshd, nginx, cron...
  |
  v
login prompt
lessons.example:
$ cat /proc/1/comm
systemd
(sample systemd-based host; containers and other init systems differ)
lessons.scenario: A server starts firmware, then bootloader, kernel and finally its init manager.

check.q: What loads before the Linux kernel in a typical PC boot?
check.e: The bootloader loads the kernel; systemd starts afterward.

lessons.title: systemctl: the remote control
lessons.body:
start / stop / restart act NOW: sudo systemctl restart nginx.

enable / disable control BOOT behavior: enable wires nginx to a target specified by its [Install] section; it does not start the service right now.

enable --now does both at once - the common answer to 'make it run and survive reboot'.

status shows running state + recent logs: systemctl status nginx. is-active and is-enabled answer yes/no questions for scripts.
lessons.example:
$ sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/nginx.service

$ systemctl is-active nginx
active
$ systemctl status nginx | head -3
* nginx.service - A high performance web server
   Active: active (running)
lessons.scenario: To run nginx now and on later boots, use systemctl enable --now nginx.

check.q: Which action starts a service immediately?
check.e: start acts now; enable arranges later target activation.

lessons.title: Unit files: services as text
lessons.body:
A service is just a text file (a 'unit'). Vendor defaults often live in /usr/lib/systemd/system/ (or /lib/systemd/system/), your overrides belong in /etc/systemd/system/.

Three sections: [Unit] describes and orders (After=network.target), [Service] says how to run (ExecStart=, Restart=), [Install] wires it to boot (WantedBy=multi-user.target).

After a unit file edit: sudo systemctl daemon-reload; restart the affected service if its running behavior must change.

mask (vs disable) forbids starting entirely - even manually - until unmask.
lessons.example:
[Unit]
Description=My backup service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/backup/run.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
lessons.scenario: Keep your local service definition under /etc/systemd/system, not in the package vendor folder.

check.q: What reloads unit definitions after editing them?
check.e: daemon-reload re-reads unit files without restarting PID 1.

lessons.title: journalctl: every log in one place
lessons.body:
systemd collects service logs into the journal. journalctl reads it.

The daily trio:
journalctl -u nginx - logs of ONE service.
journalctl -f - follow live, like tail -f.
journalctl -b - only since this boot; -b -1 shows the PREVIOUS boot (gold after a crash/reboot).

Add -p err to see only errors, --since '1 hour ago' for a time window.
lessons.example:
$ journalctl -u nginx -n 5 --no-pager
Sep 27 13:10 server nginx[820]: started
...
$ journalctl -p err -b
<- errors of this boot only
lessons.scenario: After a failed nginx startup, `journalctl -u nginx -n 20` shows recent related entries.

check.q: Which option follows new journal entries?
check.e: -f follows; -b filters to a boot.

lessons.title: SSH keys: passwords done right
lessons.body:
Good SSH key pairs are harder to guess than weak passwords, but private keys still need protection.

ssh-keygen creates a PAIR on your machine: a private key (never leaves your laptop, chmod 600) and a public key (safe to share).

ssh-copy-id user@server installs your public key into the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. After setup, SSH can authenticate with the key, though an encrypted private key may prompt for its passphrase.

Server hardening classic: PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config - then reload sshd. Test in a SECOND session before closing your first!
lessons.example:
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519
$ ssh-copy-id akash@server
$ ssh akash@server   <- may ask for your key passphrase

$ sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
$ sudo systemctl reload ssh
lessons.scenario: Keep the private SSH key on your own machine; put only the public key on the server.

check.q: Where does the public SSH key go for login?
check.e: authorized_keys permits that public key; never upload your private key.

lessons.title: cron: the robot alarm clock
lessons.body:
cron runs commands on a schedule. crontab -e edits YOUR schedule; five time fields decide when: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Cron field rules and timezone depend on the implementation; check the server clock.

0 2 * * * = 2 AM daily (backup o'clock). */5 * * * * = every 5 minutes. @daily, @weekly, @reboot are shortcuts.

System jobs live in /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.daily and friends. Scripts should use absolute paths - cron's environment is minimal.
lessons.example:
$ crontab -l
0 2 * * * /home/akash/backup.sh
(sample schedule; read-only command; output can say no crontab for user)
lessons.scenario: A nightly backup at 02:00 might use `0 2 * * * /path/to/script` in a user crontab.

check.q: How many time fields are in a normal user crontab line?
check.e: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, then command.

lessons.title: tar, gzip, rsync: pack and move
lessons.body:
tar packs many files into one archive: -czf creates gzipped, -xzf extracts, -tzf lists without extracting. Remember: Create, eXtract, lisT.

rsync is the smart copier: rsync -av /data/ server:/backup/ copies only what CHANGED and preserves permissions. It is the backbone of real backup scripts. The trailing slash matters: /data/ copies the CONTENTS, /data copies the FOLDER itself.
lessons.example:
$ tar -czf etc-backup.tar.gz /etc
$ tar -tzf etc-backup.tar.gz | head -3
etc/
etc/hostname

$ rsync -av /var/www/ backup:/srv/www/
sending incremental file list
index.html
lessons.scenario: Archive logs with tar; sync a copy to a remote host with rsync.

check.q: Which tar option lists without extracting?
check.e: t = list table; x = extract.

lessons.title: Logs, logins and least privilege
lessons.body:
/var/log is the diary of the system: auth.log (Debian) or secure (RHEL) records logins - check it after 'something feels off'. last shows login history; who shows who is on RIGHT now.

Golden rule: least privilege - every user and service gets ONLY the access it needs. Web servers run as www-data, not root; humans use sudo, not root shells.

And the habit that beats all tools: apply security updates regularly. Patches close known flaws, though updates are only one part of security.
lessons.example:
$ last | head -3
akash  pts/0  192.168.1.5  Sun Sep 27 13:00 still logged in

$ grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | wc -l
412   <- someone is knocking; consider fail2ban
lessons.scenario: When a login fails, check auth logs and apply least privilege rather than making services root.

check.q: What does least privilege mean?
check.e: Less unnecessary access means less damage if an account is compromised.
